concepts.definition: The primary vehicle for funding spending; easily created by mutual agreement of any willing parties; 'the promise to deliver money'; produces buying power that did not previously exist and leaves a lingering obligation to pay.
What credit creates: an obligation to pay back principal plus interest; 'a debt is a promise to deliver money'.

What settles transactions; once given, the transaction is complete. Anyone can create credit but only central banks can create money, in whatever amounts they choose. Under fiat (since 1971) money is what central banks print and is closer to credit (a promise of buying power, not a hard asset).

A medium of exchange that is also a storehold of wealth and cannot easily be increased in supply (gold, silver, more recently Bitcoin). Early in the cycle paper money is convertible into it at a fixed price.
Investor holdings of money earning interest (footnote 3).

The build-up of paper money and debt assets/liabilities relative to hard money, real assets and the income needed to service the debt; formally, the build-up of debt assets and liabilities over successive short-term cycles to unmanageable amounts, resolved by big restructurings and monetizations. Lasts roughly 80 years, give or take 25.

Cycle of 1) recessions, 2) central banks supplying cheap credit, 3) booms, 4) bubbles and inflations, 5) central bank tightening, 6) market and economic weakening; about six years, give or take three; each ends with more debt than the last.

The combination of five interrelated forces (Big Debt Cycle, internal political cycle, geopolitical cycle, acts of nature, new technologies) that moves from one order to the next; ends when orders break down, about once in a lifetime.
Ways of operating that change when systems break down: monetary orders, political orders (governance within countries), geopolitical orders (governance between countries).
When there have been more promises to deliver money than there is money to deliver on them.
When debt assets and debt liabilities become too large relative to the amount of money in existence and/or the goods and services in existence.
The amount a debtor must pay each year in interest and principal to avoid default.
Earnings greater than spending excluding interest payments = primary surplus; less = primary deficit (footnote 16); equivalently expenses excluding interest versus revenue.
Exists when money coming in is less than money going out, so that savings fall and/or borrowing rises until savings run out and/or no more can be borrowed, at which point a debt failure occurs.
Earnings equal to or greater than spending and debts not building faster than incomes; debt growth is healthy if the borrowed money raises incomes faster than debt service rises.
Being productive, a healthy income statement (earning more than spending) and a healthy balance sheet (more assets than liabilities).
When the free-market demand for a government's debt falls short of the supply of it; more generally when debt service becomes large relative to income and savings.
Debt and debt-service levels that cannot be prevented from accelerating without great losses to debt investors.

Self-reinforcing contraction in which the need to borrow to service debt coincides with rising rates because holding the debt/currency is seen as risky; creditors sell, rates rise further or money is printed, the currency devalues, more selling follows. For a central bank: losses and negative cash flow force printing, which requires buying more debt and more losses.
Turning in debt assets to get real money, which lenders/banks do not have enough of.

1930s phrase for the late-cycle condition in which central bank stimulus does not translate into spending because savers, investors and businesses fear borrowing and/or deflation makes risk-free cash attractive, even at or below 0% rates.

A deleveraging in which debt restructurings (deflationary) and central bank money printing/debt buying (inflationary) are balanced so that growth is positive, debt burdens fall relative to incomes and inflation is acceptable; nominal growth ends up above nominal interest rates. Only possible for debt in the country's own currency.
The central bank does not default but cannot make its debt-service payments without printing money, i.e., it has a very large negative net worth and prints to cover negative cash flow.
The late stage of the long-term debt cycle in which the central government cannot fund itself through private demand for its debt and depends on the central bank printing (the focus of ch. 2).
Phase 1: money convertible into hard money. US 1945-1971. Ends when the debt bubble bursts, a run from credit assets to hard money occurs and limited hard money causes massive defaults.

Phase 2: interest rates, bank reserves and capital requirements control credit growth. US 1971-2008. Ends when rate changes no longer work (rates at 0%) and/or private demand for debt falls short of supply.

Phase 3: central bank creates money and credit to buy investment assets (mostly bonds and mortgages, sometimes equities) when rates cannot fall further and private demand is insufficient; lifts financial asset prices, benefits asset holders, not targeted. US 2008-2020.

concepts.term: MP3 - Fiat with coordinated big fiscal deficit and big debt monetization
concepts.definition: Phase 4: fiscal and monetary policy coordinated to get money and credit to those who need it most; temporarily alleviates but does not rectify the debt problem.
A big reduction in debt and debt service via restructuring and/or monetization; at best a beautiful deleveraging.

concepts.term: Phase 6 - The Return to Hard Money
concepts.definition: After write-downs the government restores the soundness of money and credit; countries typically return to MP0 or MP1 with high real rates that benefit lender-creditors.

Net debt low, money sound, country competitive, debt growth funds productivity growth that creates incomes more than sufficient to repay; debt and debt service low relative to incomes and liquid assets; risky assets cheap relative to safe assets.

Debt and investment growth greater than can be serviced from incomes being produced; cheap money, debt-financed boom, bullish sentiment, overpriced markets, transformative inventions bought without regard to price; debt and debt-service growth exceed the income growth needed to service them.
The bubble pops and a debt/credit/market/economic contraction begins, typically from the combination of monetary tightening and an unsustainable prior rate of debt growth.

Painful bringing down of debt and debt-service levels into line with incomes so debt is sustainable; problems spread from private sector to government to central bank; defaults, restructurings and/or devaluations.
A new equilibrium is reached and a new cycle begins; requires sound money, debt in line with incomes, belief by creditors and debtors, and money/credit and real rates in line with both sides' needs.

Dalio's composite measure of bubble conditions using extended periods (e.g., three years) of debt growth significantly faster than income growth, high asset prices relative to present values of likely cash flows, and other factors; described at economicprinciples.org and the Principles In Action app.

concepts.term: Five major parts of the economic machine
concepts.definition: Goods, services and investment assets; money used to buy them; credit issued to buy them; debt liabilities created when purchases are made with credit; debt assets (deposits, bonds) that are the other side of the liabilities.

Borrower-debtors (private or government); lender-creditors (private or government); intermediaries called banks (all financial intermediaries, footnote 15); central governments; government-controlled central banks that create money and credit and influence its cost.

The debt/credit/money/economic cycle; the internal political order/disorder cycle; the external geopolitical order/disorder cycle; acts of nature (droughts, floods, pandemics); human inventiveness, especially new technologies. Selected from 18 measures in Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order.
The amount spent on something ($) divided by the total quantity of it sold (Q); P = $/Q.
The aggregate of the transactions in a thing; all markets and economies are aggregates of transactions.
An exchange of money and credit today for money and credit in the future.
Yield plus price change.
A medium of exchange and a storehold of wealth (held in debt assets); debt and currency are essentially the same thing because a debt asset is a promise to receive currency at a future date.

Spot is the price for delivery today; forward/futures is the price for future delivery; the two are linked by arbitrage (forward premium no more than storage cost including interest; for stored items like gold the spot is the expected future price minus storage cost).

concepts.term: Four levers to reduce debt burdens
concepts.definition: 1) Austerity (spending less), 2) debt defaults/restructurings, 3) the central bank printing money and making purchases or providing guarantees, 4) transfers of money and credit from those who have more to those who have less (via taxes).
Not previewed in this range; Part II's template is referenced only as the typical/archetypical sequence of events derived from 35 cases.

mechanisms.statement: One person's spending is another's earnings, so credit creation raises spending, incomes and asset prices while repayment lowers them; the credit/spending/repayment dynamic is inherently cyclical.
Governments and central banks are biased toward creating credit because the expansion phase is popular.

Short-term cycle: cheap money when activity and inflation are low and rates are low versus inflation and other returns drives borrowing, which lifts asset prices, activity and inflation until money is restrained and rates are high versus inflation and returns, which lowers borrowing, prices, growth and inflation, after which rates fall and the cycle restarts.
Because credit is a stimulant people want more of, each short-term cycle's debt highs and lows exceed the prior cycle's, so short-term cycles add up to the long-term cycle.
Early in the Big Debt Cycle debt burdens are low and productive uses plentiful so borrowing is safe; late, burdens are high and lenders have fewer productive options so default risk is high.
Early-cycle yields and expected returns on risky assets are very high relative to low-risk assets because memories of past pain shape pricing.
Short-term cycles end because of economic restraint; the long-term cycle ends because debt burdens become too great to sustain.
A short-term contraction can be reversed with a heavy dose of money and credit; a long-term contraction cannot, because debt levels are unsustainable and holders want out of debt assets.

Overborrowing proceeds from the private sector to the central government to the central bank, which prints to buy government debt and then has its own losses, monetizing more if the debt is in its currency.

When there are more promises to deliver money than money, the central bank must either print (devaluing money) or not print (default crisis); it always ends up printing, and either way debt assets lose value.
The most important variable across cases is whether the debt is denominated in a currency the central bank can print and whether it is a reserve currency.

Because a central bank can bail out a central government, the risk of government debt losing value through devaluation is hidden by default-only credit ratings; Dalio rates devaluation risk as at least as probable as default.
The Big Debt Cycle moves from sound/hard money to increasingly loose money and credit to a bust that forces a return to sound/hard money.
Bubble periods show extended debt growth significantly faster than income growth and high asset prices relative to present values of likely cash flows.

The point of no return is reached when debt and debt service cannot be stopped from accelerating without great losses to investors; the death spiral starts when borrowing is needed to service debt while rates rise because the risk of holding the debt/currency has become apparent.
The bubble pops from the combination of monetary tightening and an unsustainable prior rate of debt growth; the contraction is self-reinforcing and spreads quickly.
A debt contraction can be temporarily reversed by creating more credit and debt, until that can no longer continue and a big deleveraging occurs.
In the deleveraging stage debt problems spread from the private sector to the central government and then to the central bank.

Net selling of debt assets drives rates up, which makes the debt harder to service and riskier, driving rates higher; the central bank then supplies money and credit to fill the demand gap, lowering the value of money and credit while lowering credit risk.

Selling of government debt produces a market-driven tightening, a weaker economy, downward pressure on the currency and declining reserves as the central bank defends the currency; the central bank eventually eases and allows devaluation.

Cutting spending during a contraction raises debt-to-income ratios because spending is income; policy then shifts to a mix of restructurings and monetizations, with the mix depending on how much debt is in the local currency.
A stable equilibrium is reached through several painful adjustment spasms because borderline soundness is reached before secure soundness.

To stimulate, the central bank must push rates below nominal growth, inflation and bond rates; when rates cannot fall further, demand for government debt is short and easing is insufficient, it switches to new tools.
In the deleveraging the government's deficit widens as revenue falls and spending rises while private demand for its debt is insufficient, producing a debt squeeze that net selling makes much worse.
Central banks facing the hard/soft money choice always eventually print and devalue because repaying with hard money causes severe downturns; each can only print its own currency.

Central bank buying targets government debt and systemically important private debt to replace inadequate demand and hold rates artificially low, sometimes equities; devaluation is used because it is stimulative and raises inflation; gold links are broken and fiat follows.

Central bank actions can raise nominal rates by tightening against inflation or by not tightening so that holders refuse new issuance; real and nominal rates and the supply and demand for debt must be watched.
Extraordinary policies (extraordinary taxes, capital controls, freezing or seizing enemy assets, new forms of money) become common in the deleveraging stage.
A typical deleveraging must lower debt-to-income by roughly 50%, give or take about 20%, through defaults, restructurings and/or devaluations.

Restructurings cut debt burdens and are deflationary; monetary stimulation cuts burdens by providing money to buy debt and is inflationary; balanced, they yield positive growth with falling burdens and acceptable inflation.

A viable new cycle requires sound money, debt and debt service in line with incomes, belief by creditors and debtors, and money/credit and real rates in line with both sides' needs; credibility is restored by the government earning more than it spends and/or the central bank offering high real yields, raising reserves or linking the currency to gold or a strong currency.
The type of monetary policy in use reveals the stage of the Big Debt Cycle, because central banks must change how they operate as the cycle progresses.

A modern central bank prints by borrowing reserves from commercial banks at a very short-term rate; it loses money when the interest earned on bought debt is below what it pays on reserves; large losses force more printing, which is the central bank's death spiral and produces inflationary recessions or depressions.

Restructurings and monetizations eventually reduce debts relative to incomes and the cycle runs its course; for great empires the end of the Big Debt Cycle has typically meant the end of their prominence.
Big debt crises are inevitable because lending is never done perfectly relative to incomes and psychology amplifies the cycle (optimism in the bubble, pessimism in the bust).
If debt is in a currency the central bank cannot print, the result is defaults and deflationary depression measured in that currency.
Spreading debt reduction over time is far less traumatic: cutting debt-to-income by 50% at 3-4% per year versus 50% in one year.

Money and credit are the lifeblood, the central government the brain (using about 15-30% of money and credit) and the central bank the heart that pumps money and credit; if capital is used productively all prosper.
More money in existence allows more credit and spending, less allows less, though not exactly proportionally.
Price equals total spending divided by total quantity sold, so estimating price means estimating the two and understanding the motivations of the biggest buyers and sellers.

The conventional supply/demand-in-quantities approach wrongly assumes a single price elasticity over time; prices change because of changes in the rates of spending and quantities sold, not because of a return to equilibrium.

Debt busts are mechanical, not primarily psychological: before 2008 and 2010-12 the pace of debt buying had to slow as leveraged financial institutions hit regulatory leverage limits while debt supply rose.
Relying on confidence from controlling out-year deficits is naive because it ignores who will actually buy and sell what amounts of bonds.
If the rate of buying falls from X to X minus 10% with all else unchanged, price falls 10%; identifying unsustainable rates of buying or selling identifies unsustainable prices and conditions.
Debt/credit/economic cycles are driven more by changes in money and credit creation (spending) than by changes in quantity sold; most goods are produced in response to demand.

More money and credit with spare productive capacity gives non-inflationary growth; more money and credit without capacity gives little real growth and much inflation; hence strong growth with low inflation early in the cycle and weak growth with big price rises late.
High productivity growth lets quantity rise with money and credit, extending non-inflationary growth.
Spending on goods and services versus investments depends on the cost of goods relative to money and credit available and the relative appeal of financial assets.
All investments compete on total return (yield plus price change) because investors care about total return and can arbitrage between assets.
With Treasuries yielding X% (e.g., 5%) and gold yielding nothing, the market prices gold to rise by about X% per year relative to Treasuries.

Expected real returns, not nominal, drive allocation; when bond yields are low relative to inflation bonds are sold and inflation-hedge assets bought, and heavy money creation pushes investors toward inflation hedges.
Relative pricing of short- and long-term government debt is driven largely by the projected pace of central bank rate changes.

Debt and currency are the same thing: disliking a currency implies disliking the bonds denominated in it given relative yields, and vice versa; relative yields plus expected price changes equal relative total returns and drive capital flows.

If one country's government rate is X% below another's, its currency must be expected to appreciate X% per year; otherwise near-risk-free profits exist and investors sell the lower-yielding debt and currency.

When the expected currency move does not offset the rate gap, adjustment comes through the spot currency falling, the bond yield rising (prices falling), or under capital controls a compounding loss to holders.

From a central banker's view currency weakness and inflation can be beneficial because they reduce debt burdens when nominal rates are below nominal growth and especially below inflation (negative real rates).
Bond returns go bad through local-currency price declines as rates rise, currency declines, or interest plus currency failing to compensate for inflation.

Cross-country inflation differences are more due to changes in the values of money and currencies (from money and credit supplies) than to changes in the values of goods measured in a common currency.
Debt expansion needs willing borrower-debtors and lender-creditors, so the deal must suit both; what is good for one is often bad for the other.

Rates too high for borrowers force spending cuts, asset sales or defaults and markets and the economy fall; rates too low for lenders make them stop lending and sell debt assets, pushing rates up or forcing the central bank to print, which creates inflation and contraction in wealth.

Banks profit by borrowing cheaply and lending for more; bubbles and crises come from banks lending far more than they have, and crises occur when loans are not repaid or creditors want more back than banks can give.
Over the long run debts cannot rise faster than the incomes that service them, and rates cannot stay too high for borrowers or too low for lenders for long; it pays to watch these ratios.
Total money and credit created determines total spending on goods, services and financial assets, so all three tend to rise and fall together with money and credit.

Central banks were created to smooth cycles and handle big debt crises after runs on banks collapsed systems; they print to lend in crises, which alleviates debt problems but reduces the buying power of money and debt and raises inflation.
Central banks ease when debt growth, growth and inflation are low (favoring borrower-debtors) and tighten when they are unsustainably high (favoring lender-creditor-savers).

Central governments give people what they want without paying for it, so they borrow, reinforcing credit stimulation early and debt depressants later; the bias toward credit stimulation produces long-term uptrends in debt and debt service relative to incomes until they are too large to sustain.
The larger debt assets and liabilities are relative to real incomes, the harder the balancing act between lenders and borrowers and the greater the likelihood of a debt-caused downturn.

Two cycles (short-term about six years give or take three, long-term about 80 years give or take 25) evolve around an upward productivity trend; the short-term cycle dominates over 1-10 years, the long-term cycle and productivity over 10 years and beyond.

A debt cycle is sustainable only if the debt creates sufficient income to pay the debt service; otherwise debt-to-income grows mechanically and borrowing is needed to service debt as well as to spend.
A large and rising amount of borrowing used to pay debt service is a sure sign of movement toward a debt crisis.
Central bankers fail to contain debt because everyone wants markets up, risky debt levels are unclear in advance, forgoing credit has opportunity costs, and crises can usually be managed.
Too little credit can be as costly as too much; debt losses can be spread tolerably if the government controls the restructuring and the debt is in a currency the central bank can print.

Late in the cycle holders of debt want to sell, so debt has a bad return one way or another; the central bank chooses between not monetizing (rates rise to the level that balances bond buying and selling, cash becomes valuable, stocks and hard assets fall, deflation and defaults) and monetizing (money plentiful and devalued, inflation, other assets rise, fewer defaults); the first comes first and proves intolerable, the second eventually follows.
Big restructurings and monetizations end the prior Big Debt Cycle and its monetary order and start the next, like seismic shifts in political and world orders.

Austerity is tried first and fails because cutting debts and spending cuts incomes and net worths commensurately while revenue falls and demands rise, widening deficits; raising taxes then squeezes further.

Spending greater than revenue plus liquid liabilities greater than liquid assets create the need to borrow and sell debt assets; without enough demand this produces a deflationary or inflationary crisis.

A beautiful deleveraging restructures debts (spreading or disposing of payments) and has the central bank print and buy debt in balanced amounts, producing nominal growth (inflation plus real growth) above nominal interest rates so debt burdens fall relative to incomes.
Most big own-currency debt crises were restructured quickly, typically in one to three years.

Healthy debt: private credit for profitable uses and government borrowing for productivity gains or countercyclical support repaid later; unhealthy: the central bank chronically printing to cover the demand shortfall for debt and the government chronically running large deficits with debt and debt service rising faster than tax revenue.

At the beginning of the end of the Big Debt Cycle both the tight-money contraction and the loose-money inflation occur, only their order is uncertain, and owning the debt and currency of overly indebted governments is a bad investment.

The five forces reinforce each other: financial crises raise the odds of internal conflict, internal conflict worsens finances, and both weaken a country and, when global, raise the odds of international conflict.

The decline of great powers shows in unwavering rises of indebtedness accompanied by weakening monetary systems and declining education, infrastructure, law and order, civility and government effectiveness relative to other powers.
As debt-to-income rises, interest and rollover payments rise each year, creating rollover risk and higher debt service as a share of income that crowds out spending.
As debt service rises relative to income investors expect credit problems, lend less and sell debt assets, which brings the credit problems about.

Nominal rates relative to inflation and nominal growth determine how debt and debt service grow relative to income and how attractive lending is relative to borrowing; high rates relative to growth and inflation favor lenders and discourage borrowing and signal risk among debtors who cannot print.
Large savings or reserves prevent default risk from being high even when the other ratios are unhealthy.
The four key ratios indicate how likely and how severe a debt squeeze will be but not exactly when, because lead times for selling and other precipitating actions differ.
Rising rates raise interest costs only gradually as bonds roll into new rates; stressed debtors see maturities shorten, which raises principal payments for the same debt level.

When rates rise above revenue growth both the debt level and the rate rise, so interest costs (their product) and debt service grow faster than debt; when rates fall, debt grows slowly and debt service shrinks (Japan over the last 20 years).

Issuance need equals the primary deficit plus interest plus maturing principal; if buyers are unwilling at current rates, rates rise until someone buys, which worsens the deficit and the desire to sell (the death spiral); rising rates also constrict income growth, and forced extra issuance (war, recession benefits) drives rates up much more.

Governments under squeeze are the largest part of the economy and the only payer of large non-economic social expenses, so cutting spending then deepens the downturn, worsens debt burdens via lower incomes and net worths, and can cause social turmoil; fights over taxes and left/right conflict follow.

Private demand for government debt depends on expected real bond returns versus other assets, total money and credit, and the sense of impending crisis; it shows up as rates rising while the economy and currency are weak, or as the central bank spending reserves and printing to buy debt.

Monetization: the central bank creates reserves/cash and exchanges it for bonds, raising M0; the more private demand falls short at the rates needed, the more the central bank must buy and the more money it creates, which devalues money and makes holding debt less attractive.
All else equal, central bank money and credit creation lowers the value of money, raising inflation and weakening the currency; the relationship is imprecise and depends on transmission.

Lowering rates weakens the spot currency because long-run (10-year forward) currency expectations barely move, so lower interim interest must be offset by a lower spot that appreciates toward the same forward point.

A rise in one country's 10-year risk-free yield relative to another's raises its 10-year forward currency; the interest differential is offset by the forward premium (2% higher rate equals a 2% per year forward discount), so cutting rates by 1% with the forward fixed weakens the spot correspondingly.
Printed money can flow directly out of the currency as bond sellers buy other currencies, adding selling pressure.
The worse a currency is viewed as a storehold of value, the more sensitive it is to money supply growth; sensitivity rises as private players become less willing to lend.

A central bank can prevent debt service from rising, or make it fall, relative to inflation and incomes by pushing nominal rates below nominal growth, at the cost of lower nominal and real returns for lender-creditors.

Historically a mix of the four levers is used, with a strong bias to print money and buy debt when the squeeze is big; the easiest path is for the central bank to print and buy bonds to hold rates at tolerable levels, which governments unfailingly do when debts are in their own currency.

equations.name: Price identity
equations.expression: P = $ / Q, where $ = total amount spent and Q = total quantity sold
equations.explanation: Price of any good, service or financial asset equals total spending by buyers divided by total quantity sold; estimate price by estimating the two and the motivations of the big buyers and sellers. A 10% fall in the rate of buying, all else equal, lowers price 10%.

equations.name: Total return
equations.expression: total return = yield + price change
equations.explanation: All investment markets derive value from yield and price change and compete on total return.

equations.name: Gold versus bonds pricing
equations.expression: expected gold appreciation ≈ Treasury yield X% (e.g., 5%)
equations.explanation: Since gold has no yield, it is bought only if expected to rise by more than the bond yield; the market therefore prices gold to rise ~X% per year relative to Treasuries.

equations.name: Interest parity (currency vs rate differential)
equations.expression: if rate_A = rate_B − X% per year, then expected appreciation of currency A = X% per year
equations.explanation: Otherwise near-risk-free profits exist and investors sell the lower-yielding debt/currency; the rate difference is eaten by the higher-rate currency falling.

equations.name: Worked currency example
equations.expression: A's 10-yr rate 3% below B's while A's currency expected to fall 2%/yr → spot falls ~40%, or A's 10-yr rate rises 5% (bond prices −~40%), or under capital controls a 5%/yr loss compounding to ~40% over 10 years
equations.explanation: Footnote 11: 2% depreciation for 10 years gives a forward at 82% of the current price; the spot must fall to 0.61 because 0.61 × 1.03^10 = 0.82. Footnote 12: bond price impact = change in yield × duration; 10-year government bond duration 7-8 years; 8 × 5% = 40%.

equations.name: Formula 1: Future debt relative to future income
equations.expression: Future Debt / Future Revenue = [(Future Expenses Excluding Interest − Future Revenue) + Current Debt × (1 + Interest Rate)] / [Current Revenue × (1 + Growth Rate)]
equations.explanation: Future debt-to-revenue depends on 1) spending more or less than revenue (primary balance), 2) compounding of existing debt at the interest rate, 3) revenue growth. Uses revenue rather than GDP because GDP matters only if taxed. Can be rearranged to solve for the deficit, rate or growth that keeps the ratio flat.

equations.name: Debt dynamics identity (footnote 17)
equations.expression: Debt/Income_t − Debt/Income_(t−1) = (i_t − g_t) × Debt/Income_(t−1) + (Primary Deficit/Income)_t
equations.explanation: g = income growth rate, i = interest rate, t = year. The change in debt-to-income equals the rate-growth gap times the prior ratio plus the primary deficit share.

equations.name: Primary balance that holds debt-to-income constant
equations.expression: Primary Deficit / Income = (g − i) × Debt / Income
equations.explanation: To keep debt constant relative to income, the primary deficit as a share of income must equal the growth-minus-interest gap multiplied by the current debt-to-income ratio.

equations.name: Formula 2: Future debt service relative to future income
equations.expression: Future Debt Service / Future Revenue = (Future Interest Costs + Future Principal Payments) / [Current Revenue × (1 + Growth Rate)]
equations.explanation: If revenue grows a lot, debt service falls relative to income, all else equal.

equations.name: Future interest costs
equations.expression: Future Interest Costs = Future Debt Level × Average Effective Interest Rate on Debt
equations.explanation: Rate rises feed through gradually as bonds roll into new rates.

equations.name: Future principal payments
equations.expression: Future Principal Payments = Future Debt Level × Share of Debts Coming Due
equations.explanation: Rough estimate from average maturity of existing debt; maturities shorten as creditors become stressed, raising principal payments.

equations.name: Formula 3: Interest rate required to keep debt flat
equations.expression: Interest Rate Required to Keep Debt Flat = Revenue Growth Rate − (Future Expenses Excluding Interest − Future Revenue) / Starting Debt Level
equations.explanation: With zero primary deficit, debt stays flat when the interest rate equals revenue growth; with a primary deficit of 5% of the current debt level, rates must be 5% below revenue growth.

equations.name: Formula 4a: Future debt relative to future savings
equations.expression: Future Debt / Future Savings = [(Current Expenses Excluding Interest − Current Revenue) + Current Debt × (1 + Interest Rate)] / [Current Savings + Expected Savings]
equations.explanation: Same structure as Formula 1 but relative to savings/reserves; large savings buffer debt burdens. Footnote 18 notes the equation is inexact because a surplus could reduce debt or raise savings.

equations.name: Formula 4b: Future debt service relative to future savings
equations.expression: Future Debt Service / Future Savings = (Future Interest Costs + Future Principal Payments) / (Current Savings + Expected Savings)
equations.explanation: Debt service relative to the savings buffer; consistent deficits with negative expected surplus make debt grow quickly relative to savings.

equations.name: One-year compounding example
equations.expression: debt 100% of income, nominal rate 5%, nominal income growth 3%, spending = income → debt ≈ 102% of income next year
equations.explanation: Illustrates how the rate-growth gap raises debt-to-income even without a primary deficit.

equations.name: Rule of thumb: 2-point rate-growth gap over 20 years
equations.expression: i − g = +2% with zero primary deficit → debt/income rises ~50% over 20 years (50% → 75%; 400% → 600%)
equations.explanation: Consistent with 1.02^20 ≈ 1.49; the nominal rate versus nominal growth gap is called probably the single most important variable.

equations.name: Deleveraging magnitude
equations.expression: required fall in debt-to-income ≈ 50% ± ~20%; spread at 3-4% per year rather than 50% in one year
equations.explanation: Typical size of the debt-to-income reduction in a deleveraging and the pacing that makes it less traumatic.

equations.name: Example 1: US baseline debt path (rates = growth)
equations.expression: primary deficit ≈ 12% of income (expenses ex-interest ≈ 112% of income); interest borrowing ≈ 20% of income per year; debt/income 580% → 700% over 10 years (+120 points)
equations.explanation: Uses CBO baseline (settled law; Trump tax cuts expire; extension adds 1.5% of GDP or 8% of revenue per year). Grid cell = starting ratio + 10 × primary deficit.

equations.name: Example 2: US path with CBO rate-growth gap
equations.expression: effective rate 3.45%, nominal growth 3.9%, gap ≈ −0.4%, total deficit 32% of income (12% primary) → debt/income ≈ 650% after 10 years
equations.explanation: Grid of 10-year debt-to-income by starting ratio and (nominal rate − nominal growth) with a 12% primary deficit; at 600% start and 0% gap the result is 720%, at −1% gap 660%.

equations.name: Example 3: Year-1 issuance need in the toy model
equations.expression: revenue $5.4T; spending $6.0T (32% above income incl. interest; 12% primary deficit); interest $1T (3.5% on debt = 580% of income); maturing 35% of $30.1T ≈ $10.5T; total to sell ≈ $12.2T
equations.explanation: Inputs: income growth 3.9%, spending ex-interest 112% of income, starting debt $30.1T, starting rate 3.5%, 35% maturing per year (about the US share).

equations.name: Example 3 outcome: rates +50bp/yr with flat nominal growth
equations.expression: Year 10: debt 865% of income, interest 67% of income, total debt service 342% of income; versus flat rates: debt 650%, interest 22%

stages.name: The Private Sector and Government Get Deep in Debt
entry_conditions: Large and growing stock of government debt from chronic deficit spending (p. 106)
Rising share of spending to consumption/social safety net, falling share to productivity-enhancing investment; safety net a political third rail (Brazil, US today) (p. 106)
Debt high relative to tax-revenue capacity; debt service high relative to income and crowding out essential spending (p. 106)
More debt must be sold than the private sector wants to buy, pushing rates up (p. 106)
Heavy private borrowing that the public sector must back (implicit bank guarantees) counts as a public balance-sheet problem (p. 108)
Buildup financed by large foreign lending in local currency (devaluation risk) or reserve currency (default risk) (p. 108)
Steadily rising current-account and twin deficits lead the crisis by several years (p. 109)
Substantial accumulated net debt to foreigners; few liquid assets vs external obligations by devaluation (p. 110)
dynamics: Fixed-rate cases: more severe, definitive restructuring and a more abrupt, larger rebound; fiat cases: gradual rise in debt as printing lets spending continue (p. 106)
Large, persistent government deficits in 31 of 35 cases going into the crisis (p. 107)
Current-account deficit alone is not a problem; becomes a vulnerability when the country must issue lots of debt and money quickly (p. 109)
Crisis takes the form of a big devaluation and a constriction of debt-financed demand incl. imports, which shrinks the deficits (p. 109)
Ex-ongoing charts exclude US, Europe, UK, Japan post-financial-crisis as cases still playing out (fn. 22, p. 107)

indicators.name: Govt debt level (% revenue)
indicators.reading_or_threshold: all cases ~400% rising to ~500% at crisis peak; fixed ~620% peak; floating ~350% (chart p. 107)

indicators.name: Govt interest expense (% revenue)
indicators.reading_or_threshold: all ~20% to ~27% at peak; fixed to ~35% (chart p. 107)

indicators.name: Primary deficit (% GDP)
indicators.reading_or_threshold: ~-2 to -3% trough before peak; ~+1% surplus by +80 months (chart p. 108)

indicators.name: Non-financial private debt (% GDP)
indicators.reading_or_threshold: ~75% to ~90% at peak then falling; fixed to ~55% by +120; floating rises to ~100%+ (chart p. 108)

indicators.name: Current account (% GDP)
indicators.reading_or_threshold: ~0 to ~-2.5% over the 100 months before the peak (chart p. 109)

indicators.reading_or_threshold: ~-3% to ~-7% at peak (chart p. 109)

indicators.name: Foreign purchases of debt assets (% GDP)
indicators.reading_or_threshold: ~+2-3% in run-up, falling to ~0 (all) / ~-2.5% (fixed) just after peak (chart p. 109)

indicators.reading_or_threshold: ~8-10% rising to ~17-20% around peak (chart p. 110)

policy_responses: Continued deficit spending; safety net untouchable (p. 106)
stages.duration: Builds over several years; rising current-account and twin deficits lead the crisis by several years (p. 109); charts span 120 months before the peak
stages.transition_signal: Private sector reaches the limit of its ability to carry debt, forcing the government to step in (pp. 111-112)
stages.markets: Upward pressure on interest rates from excess supply of government debt (p. 106); foreign inflows still strong (~2-3% GDP) but about to turn (p. 109)

stages.name: The Private Sector Suffers a Debt Crisis, and the Central Government Gets Deeper in Debt to Help the Private Sector
entry_conditions: Government balance sheet goes from moderately stretched to extremely stretched as it is forced to address private-sector debt problems (p. 111)
dynamics: Government takes the larger role because it can get money and credit more easily: central bank can print and route money to it, and it can tax; most true for established reserve-currency governments (p. 111)
Government debt rises faster than private debt; private debt plunges about a year before the crisis; seen in 15 of 21 cases with data on both balance sheets (p. 111)
Government debt problems intensify: stock of debt grows relative to revenues, hard assets (reserves) and the quantity of money, until the central bank steps in (p. 112)

indicators.name: Government vs non-financial private debt (% GDP)
indicators.reading_or_threshold: government ~70% to ~95% peak just after 0; private ~80% peak just before 0 then falls; 'private sector at limits of ability to support higher debt burdens... forcing government to step in and borrow/spend' (chart p. 112)

indicators.reading_or_threshold: trough ~75% at -40 months, rising to ~105-110% (all), ~140% (fixed), ~95% (floating) (chart p. 112)

indicators.reading_or_threshold: a short leading indicator of trouble (p. 111)

indicators.name: Reserves / government debt
indicators.reading_or_threshold: ~10-11% to ~4-5% at 0; 'falling reserve coverage... until CB lets FX go' (chart p. 113)

indicators.reading_or_threshold: ~800% to ~1,100% peak just after 0; 'surge in debt, first without monetization... then monetization inevitably needed' (chart p. 113)

policy_responses: Government borrows and spends to backstop the private sector (p. 112)
stages.duration: Private debt plunge about one year before the crisis (p. 111)
stages.transition_signal: Free-market demand for the government's debt falls short of its supply (p. 113)
stages.markets: Not separately described; the signal is the balance-sheet crossover (private debt falling, government debt rising) (p. 111)

stages.name: The Central Government Experiences a Debt Squeeze in Which the Free-Market Demand for Its Debt Falls Short of the Supply of It
entry_conditions: Government finances squeezed by debt and debt-service expense that limit essential spending (p. 113)
Holders of the debt assets want to sell them (p. 113)
dynamics: Squeeze is a debt problem; net selling of the debt makes it much worse and is a big red flag (pp. 100, 113)
Upward pressure on rates raises financing costs, requiring painful spending cuts or more borrowing (p. 113)
Debt service at a very high share of income (e.g., 100%) squeezes out spending and/or requires rollovers that lender-creditors may refuse (pp. 113-114)
Debt service as % of revenues accelerated going into the crisis in 25 of 35 cases (p. 114)
At devaluation the government is typically on a path toward indefinitely rising debt and debt service absent devaluation (pp. 114-115)
Two exits: a monetary/fiscal shift that rebalances supply and demand, or self-reinforcing net selling and a severe liquidation crisis (p. 100)
Classic next step: papering over with creative financing and accounting tricks (p. 115)
US not yet there but moving toward it; Europe/Japan/China interest service ~half the US as % GDP; Japan ~215% debt/GDP could become a problem if refinanced at higher rates (p. 115)

indicators.name: Govt debt service (% revenue), accelerating
indicators.reading_or_threshold: ~100% of income is a red flag (p. 113); all cases ~115% at peak, fixed ~140% (chart p. 114)

indicators.name: Projected govt debt path (% GDP) at devaluation
indicators.reading_or_threshold: ~80% at 0 projected to ~100%+ within 10 years (chart p. 115)

indicators.name: Projected interest costs (% revenue) at devaluation
indicators.reading_or_threshold: ~25% at 0 projected to ~35% within 10 years (chart p. 115)

indicators.name: Net selling of government debt
indicators.reading_or_threshold: present = big red flag (pp. 100, 113)

indicators.name: Use of creative financing measures
indicators.reading_or_threshold: policy banks, guarantees, captive domestic buyers, patriotic campaigns, promised future cuts, creditor favors, maturity shortening, capital controls (pp. 116-117)

policy_responses: Policy and development banks for off-balance-sheet financing (Japan, Asian crises) (p. 116)
Debt guarantees instead of direct spending (Peru 1980s; Turkey 2017 loan-guarantee program) (p. 116)
Requiring/incentivizing domestic banks, pensions, insurers to hold government debt; favorable regulatory treatment; yield-curve manipulation (US WWII) = backdoor monetary financing (p. 116)
Patriotic campaigns (Turkey sell dollars for lira; WWII bond drives; Korea 1990s gold campaign for the IMF) (p. 116)
'Paying' with future cuts/tax rises that may never come (Brazil constitutional spending cap) (p. 116)
Calling in favors from international creditors / geopolitical financing deals (Turkey; UK Sterling Area post-WWII) (p. 116)
Shortening debt maturities (pp. 116-117)
Capital controls in relatively severe situations (p. 117)
stages.transition_signal: Selling of the debt becomes large enough to drive a free-market tightening of money and credit (p. 117)
stages.markets: Rates under upward pressure; yield-curve management to make government debt artificially attractive; maturities shortening (p. 116)

stages.name: The Selling of the Government's Debt Leads to a) a Free-Market-Driven Tightening of Money and Credit, Which Leads to b) a Weakening of the Economy [heading continues, paraphrased: c) downward pressure on the currency, d) declining reserves as the central bank defends the currency] (p. 117)
entry_conditions: Net selling of government debt tightens money and credit via the market; central bank attempts to defend the currency with tightening and reserve sales (p. 117)

Failure stage 1 (conditions): large gaps in wealth and values; bad and worsening conditions; weak, fragmented leadership in a republic-style representative democracy (p. 172)

Failure stage 2 (breakdown of compromise): sides willing to fight to win at all costs; intensifying populist conflict among hard right, weak middle, hard left; fights for the power to control, especially in economic stress (p. 172)

Failure stage 3 (decadence/legitimacy loss): leaders appeal to immediate benefits over systemic fixes; leadership weak, decadent, corrupt after prosperity; growing corruption, inequality, institutional failure; system loses legitimacy ('losing the mandate of heaven', China from 1046 BCE; Plato) (p. 172)

Failure stage 4 (demagogue): manipulates opinion, promises easy solutions, uses propaganda and bullying; hard-right demagogues backed by the rich/powerful (nobles, capitalists), left demagogues by the unprivileged masses; tactics of propaganda, coercion, consolidation of power to undermine enemies and democratic institutions/bureaucracies (p. 173)

Failure stage 5 (autocracy): replacement of democracy with a centralized dictatorial government, usually within the democracy's rules, becoming increasingly extreme over about three to five years; leaders make radical changes to monetary, political and geopolitical orders and become nationalistic, militaristic, expansionist and autocratic (p. 174)
Examples: Caesar 49-44 BCE; Napoleon 1799-1815; Mussolini 1922-1943; Hitler 1933-1945; Japan consortium 1931-1945; Franco 1936-1975; Erdogan 2016-now (pp. 171-172, 174)
Controls that limit autocracy: oversight functions and separation of powers (board/regulators for companies) (p. 173)
Dated: such shifts are now taking place, mostly toward the hard right (p. 174)
Note: no numbered internal-cycle stages are given in this chapter; fn. 27 defers to ch. 5 of Principles for Dealing with the Changing World Order (p. 170)
external_order_stages: Alternation between periods of order (harmony, productivity, prosperity) and disorder (great conflict, destruction, depression) between countries; disorder = fights over which country sets the order; no effective global governance makes the world order more prone to disorder (pp. 174-175)
Big swings between unilateralism (self-interest, strong over weak, law of the jungle) and multilateralism (global harmony, peaceful coexistence, egalitarianism) (p. 175)

Multilateralism has only worked after wars, when people were sick of fighting and a dominant power enforced it; brutal unilateralism is the historical norm; sustained multilateral periods extremely rare (p. 175)

Markers: Peace of Westphalia 1648; League of Nations after WWI (failed); post-WWII American order with UN, IMF, World Bank, WHO, WTO, ICJ, WIPO, US as linchpin promoting democracy, free markets, human rights; has so far prevented another world war (p. 175)

Current: multilateralism fading into irrelevance, unilateralism rising; multilateral organizations' power declining rapidly and shifting to major powers; 'the strong prey on the weak'; transition shocking then quickly normalized (Trump on Greenland/Canada/Panama Canal; Russia-Ukraine) (p. 176)
Alliances change fast as circumstances change; winning matters more than loyalty (p. 176)

Long arc: tribes seize wealth; winners grow rich, civilized, then decadent and weak; taken down by stronger barbarians (Rome/Gauls; dynasties); alternating ages of barbarism and civility produce wars when barbarians are strong and civilizations weak (pp. 176-177)
Peaceful modern version = business competition/creative destruction; destructive version = non-cooperation in politics, geopolitics, acts of nature (climate), technology (p. 177)
Note: no numbered external-cycle stages are enumerated in this chapter
acts_of_nature: Historically killed more people than wars and toppled more orders than the other forces (p. 177)

Droughts, floods and pandemics are increasing and increasingly costly; causes include pollution/disruption of nature, population density, international travel, land development bringing animal-human disease; LA wildfires; almost certain to get worse (p. 177)

Interactions: migration pressures in developed countries; worsening living conditions in underdeveloped countries; nearly all nations face debt issues so there isn't enough money for climate mitigation/adaptation (pp. 177-178)
human_inventiveness: Advances, particularly in AI, will dramatically affect all thinking in all areas for good or bad (p. 178)
Technology raises living standards and life expectancy, builds economic and military power, and causes destruction in wars; advances faster under good financial/economic/social conditions (p. 178)

Financed by unsustainable credit growth it produces bubbles and busts: South Sea Bubble 1720 (Dutch Empire beginning to decline), Railway Mania 1830s-1840s, electricity/utilities bubbles ('War of the Currents') 1870s-1890s, dot-com and telecoms crash 1990-2001 (p. 178)
gauges: Debt cycle: debt-service payments relative to income; new debt sold relative to demand for it; desirability/willingness of holders to keep holding debt assets (p. 167)
Debt cycle: position within the ~6-year short-term and ~80-year long-term cycles, estimated from monitorable influences (p. 167)
Debt cycle: whether the debt/money, internal-order and external-order forces are all late in their cycles (p. 168)
Internal order: wealth and values gaps; bad and worsening conditions; strength/fragmentation of leadership (p. 172)
Internal order: whether compromise is functioning; populist polarization (hard right / weak middle / hard left) (p. 172)
Internal order: the economy's state via the debt cycles, plus exogenous shocks (p. 171)
Internal order: the leader's honeymoon-to-disappointment arc within a term (p. 171)
Internal order: corruption, inequality, institutional effectiveness and legitimacy (p. 172)
Internal order: presence of oversight and separation of powers as controls on a would-be autocrat (p. 173)
Internal order: pace of extremization in a democracy-to-autocracy transfer (typically three to five years) (p. 174)
External order: existence of a dominant power able to enforce order (p. 175)
External order: direction of the unilateral/multilateral pendulum and the power of multilateral institutions (p. 176)
External order: speed of alliance changes (p. 176)
External order: relative strength vs decadence of the leading power (barbarism/civility arc) (pp. 176-177)
Acts of nature: frequency and cost of droughts, floods, pandemics; fiscal capacity for mitigation/adaptation (pp. 177-178)
Technology: whether advances are financed by sustainable or unsustainable credit growth (bubble risk) (p. 178)
Overarching: whether people deal with problems together or fight (p. 179)

cases.name: United States 1865-1945
cases.mechanism: Civil War debt (2%->40% of GDP) resolved by suspending gold convertibility, printing greenbacks (gold to ~$250/oz, 80% inflation in 1865); then a post-war productivity miracle financed by debt and equity (1870-1914) producing great wealth gaps and left/right conflict; with no central bank and a gold-fixed dollar, busts (1873, 1893, 1907) were long and deep, leading to the Fed in 1913; classic late-cycle symptoms 1900-14; WWI makes the US the top creditor; 1920s bubble; 1929 bust; 1933 gold default and ~40% devaluation with rates at 0% and money printing; 1930s hard-right/hard-left fights, strongman unilateralism, Versailles defaults, economic warfare and military buildups leading to WWII and the 1945 order.
stage_sequence: war debt bust resolved by devaluation/default (1865)
bubbles/busts with wealth gaps and no central bank (1873-1907)
new order (1945), now in its late stages
lessons: Too much debt relative to money forces governments to break promises via more money/credit, restructuring, and restricting hard money
Without a central bank, busts are not cushioned and can last decades
Weak countries are exploited by rivals
Gold-standard breakdowns (1865, 1933) are classic and recur
analogies_to_today: 1930s rightist turn, squaring off against leftists, retreat from multilateralism and strongman unilateralism is 'just as we are now seeing in the US and several other countries' (p. 193)
The template has worked the same way for thousands of years (p. 185)

cases.name: United States 1945-1971 (MP0, hard money)
cases.mechanism: Bretton Woods gold-dollar link with the US holding ~2/3 of world gold; citizens barred from gold so savings go to debt assets; US overspends on Vietnam and the war on poverty and borrows; foreigners initially accumulate dollars; Germany and Japan recover and US balance of payments worsens; paper claims far exceed gold; runs on US and UK central banks (de Gaulle 1965); selling drives rates up and currency down; Nixon suspends convertibility Aug 15, 1971, producing devaluation, inflation, easier debt repayment and rallies in stocks and gold, an exact repeat of 1933.
stage_sequence: early expansion with five short-term cycles (1945-1965)
inflation 3.8% and first yield-curve inversion since 1929 (1965-66)
lessons: Hard-money systems never worked long term because governments still over-create money and debt (p. 214)
When a debt problem is intolerably painful, central banks print and devalue money and debt vs other assets (p. 221)
Markets move on cash flows, not headlines; most brinkmanship ends with leaders stepping back, but insure against the rare blow-up (p. 218-219)
Investors who have only known equity bull markets misread regime changes (p. 217)
UK's post-war devaluations (1949 30%, 1967, 1976 IMF) are the classic reserve-currency decline (p. 216-217)
analogies_to_today: UK devaluation sequence 'important to keep in mind when looking at the US now' (p. 216)
Taiwan's chips today are even more important than oil was in the last cycle (p. 216)
Small seeds (tech, China opening) grow into big forces (p. 219)

cases.name: United States 1971-2008 (MP1, fiat interest-rate policy)
cases.mechanism: Fiat money steered by interest rates. 1971-81 monetization (money +100%, M2 +180%, CPI +140%, gold 10x, bonds -40% real, stocks -45% real), two oil shocks, negative real rates to -4%, labor share to 74%, left-leaning governments; voter revolt brings Volcker (1979) and Reagan/Thatcher/Kohl; 1980s high real rates, falling inflation and nominal rates, wider margins, lower taxes produce strong developed-market assets and EM inflationary depressions (1982 crisis, lost decade, 1991 resolution); Plaza Accord 1985; Soviet collapse; globalization and China's rise; internet; 1995-99 bubble; March 2000 burst (Nasdaq -80%); 9/11; easing; 2006-07 mortgage/bank bubble; 2008 crisis and rates to 0%.
stage_sequence: 1971-82 stagflation, tightening, left-to-right swing (two short-term cycles: 1971-74, 1975-80)
1982-90 disinflation, strong growth, levering up; EM debt busts
1990-2000 more disinflation and leveraging into a bubble
2000-08 bust -> deleveraging -> releveraging -> new bubble -> GFC and monetization
1981-2008: four short-term cycles with each rate high and low lower than the prior until 0%
lessons: Fiat money is the easiest and subtlest way for governments to relieve debt burdens and confiscate wealth (p. 225)
Watch capital flows; diversify; be humble (1982 mistake, p. 232)
Decades tend to be opposites of their predecessors (p. 195, 231)
Real yield plus yield curve determine whether to be a debtor or creditor (p. 203)
Everything seems bigger up close (p. 239)
Great companies are not great investments at any price; bubbles burst when central banks tighten (p. 241)
Bridgewater rule: with a debt contraction and short rates near 0%, bet on a bad contraction until policy turns very stimulative as in March 1933 (p. 242)
Policy prescription: ~2% real 10-yr yield (+/-1%) and short rate ~1% below / ~70% of long rate (p. 204)
analogies_to_today: China funding US deficits repeated the Japan pattern (p. 244)
Private credit today is the modern-day junk bond market of the late 1970s/early 1980s (p. 264)
Congress was far more bipartisan then than now (p. 244)
Clinton's surplus is a case to remember for handling debt (p. 241)

cases.name: United States 2008-2020 (MP2, debt monetization)
cases.mechanism: Mortgage-led deleveraging spreads to banks, companies and individuals (unemployment 10%, stocks -50%); rates hit 0% so MP1 is exhausted; the Fed prints and buys debt (first time since 1933) and becomes the big creditor willing to run losses; quick response gives quick rebound; asset prices up, yields down, the rich benefit; bailouts breed resentment; imports and technology hollow out the middle class; populism of right and left; Trump 2016; aggressive nationalist protectionist shift; unemployment 3.5% by end-2019; COVID. Europe follows the template with Greece unable to print: nine-step playbook ending in a Troika restructuring (~50% of GDP in 2012) and capital controls (2015).
stage_sequence: MP2 era with two short-term cycles, each with more debt creation and monetization than the prior (p. 248)
private deleveraging while government levers up ('beginning of the Big Cycle's late stage', p. 197)
wealth-gap populism and domestic order shift (2016)
Greece: deep debt -> private crisis -> govt squeeze -> selling/austerity (rates >70%) -> ECB printing -> (no CB losses) -> restructuring -> bank run/taxes/capital controls -> stabilization in euro
lessons: When rates hit zero the central bank must replace inadequate private demand for debt (p. 245-246)
The 2008-20 recovery kicked the public-debt can down the road (p. 249)
Countries that cannot print take the explicit-restructuring route, usually more painful and drawn-out (p. 254)
Central bank losses arise when it holds fixed-rate bonds financed by floating-rate reserves and must raise rates (p. 253)
Central banks of US/Europe/Japan own ~15/30/40% of government debt and ~5/10/20% of total debt (p. 246)
analogies_to_today: Post-2016 political shifts analogous to pre-WWI/WWII and the early 1930s (p. 250-251)
Post-2008 geopolitical resets analogous to 1933-38 (p. 254)

cases.name: United States 2020-now (MP3, monetized fiscal deficits)
cases.mechanism: Pandemic triggers coordinated fiscal deficits monetized by the Fed (MP3), used because MP1/MP2 no longer reach most people; debt sales far exceed free-market demand; 10-yr to 0.5% nominal / -1% real; bubble indicator 75%; paper wealth $32T -> $99T; inflation surge (plus supply chains and conflict) leads to tightening from late 2021 (yields >4% nominal / 2.5% real; bubble indicator 35%; bubble stocks -75%; wealth -12% nominal / -18% real; FAANG -45%; Nasdaq -33%); the economy is not hurt much because the government, not the private sector, holds the debt and the Fed eats the losses; inflation falls but prices stay high; modest easing; AI becomes the new hot thing; private credit keeps spreads low; 2024 Trump win; five forces intensify.
stage_sequence: long-term: leveraging-up phase, not yet deleveraging (p. 197); MP3 late in the long-term debt cycle (p. 256); ~two-thirds through the 13th short-term cycle since 1945 (p. 197); domestic order at the 1930s stage (p. 266); near the end of the current orders and Big Cycle (p. 213)
lessons: Nearly every sacrosanct rule is tested by reality and breaks down later in the Big Cycle (p. 255)
Debt service at 100% of revenue projected to 150% requires belief in rollover, new sales and no holder selling (p. 199)
Foreign and bank holders have become sellers; future demand depends on US conduct, sanctions risk, returns and prominence (p. 206-207)

Fed MTM losses ($700B, 2.5% GDP) are a red flag that becomes a problem if US debt is sold, forcing intolerable rate rises or printing/devaluation and threatening central-bank independence (p. 208-209)
Real bond yield returned to its ~2% long-run average with an inverted curve (p. 257-258)
Labor share at its lowest since the 1950s; wealth and income shares of the non-college-educated keep falling (p. 259-260)
analogies_to_today: 'This looks quite like the 1930s period' (p. 266)
2020 bubble analogous to Nifty Fifty 1970-72, Japan 1989-90, dot-com 1999-2000 (p. 262)
US-China squaring off looks like the 1930s (p. 280)

cases.name: China 1945/49-now
cases.mechanism: Century of Humiliation (1839-1949) shapes leaders' psyche; 1945-49 civil war wipes out old debts; Mao's isolated communism 1949-76; Soviet threat drives 1972 US-China friendship; Deng 1978 reform/open door yields cheap manufacturing exports with earnings lent back to the US (trade/capital imbalances); 1989 capital markets begin; 2008 crisis and G20 stimulus; from 2009 China ramps debt in real estate, local governments and companies (one-child demographics, quantity-over-profit lending); Xi 2012 reform/anti-corruption then consolidation; 2015 '2025 plan'; 2017-18 conflict in earnest; COVID; 2021 debt bubble bursts; Oct 2022 third term with Mao-like turn; four of five forces now threatening. Per-capita income 20x since 1984, life expectancy +12 years, poverty 81% -> <1%. Total debt ~290% of GDP (approx, chart).
stage_sequence: development of capital markets and its version of capitalism
classic debt bust of the own-currency, domestic-creditor type (deleveraging since 2021; 'late part of the Big Debt Cycle most analogous to Japan in the 1990s', p. 282)
lessons: Local-currency, domestically held debt allows a beautiful deleveraging, which China has been slow to engineer and Japan failed to do (p. 282, 287)
The renminbi is not a reserve currency, so it is not an effective storehold of wealth (p. 284)
Nominal bond rates near zero mean unconventional fiscal/monetary policies will likely be needed (p. 286)
Liquidity rising without a real rebound is pushing on a string (p. 287)
Real yields ~0.5% are unattractive normally, attractive vs deflation, unattractive vs the US (p. 285)
Non-debt-burdened sectors flourish; Chinese assets are now very cheap (p. 288)
Chinese leaders know the Big Cycle well and see the US as trying to contain them (p. 269-270)
analogies_to_today: China now resembles Japan in the 1990s (p. 282, 284, 287)
US-China squaring off resembles the 1930s (p. 280)
Chinese leaders view Taiwan as more intrusive than Americans viewed Cuba in the 1960s (p. 269)
Both countries face the same five issues in parallel (p. 279-280)
Xi's '100-year storm' (p. 278)

cases.name: Japan
cases.mechanism: Pre-1945: Perry 1853 -> Meiji 1868 -> wins vs China/Russia -> 1912-26 democracy -> debt crisis plus dysfunction -> hard-right military takeover -> sanctions/asset freezes/oil embargo -> Pearl Harbor -> defeat with all money and debt destroyed. 1945-90: rebuilt to the second-largest economy with a huge debt-funded bubble bursting 1989-90. 1990-2013: the opposite of a beautiful deleveraging (no restructuring for nine years, no rates below growth/inflation for 23 years, zombie institutions, rigid costs) -> deflation and stagnation; aging. 2013-: Kuroda/Abe three arrows -> massive monetization (BoJ holds >90% of GDP of JGBs), deficits 5% of GDP, rates 0.9% below growth and 1% below inflation, yen depreciation -> debt service falls, ex-BoJ debt falls, government net worth improves in dollars, workers 58% cheaper vs US, FDI rises, equities cheapen -> cost borne by bondholders and savers (JGBs -45% vs UST, -60% vs gold; yen holders -29%/-84%; Japanese ~60% poorer per capita in dollars).
stage_sequence: Big Debt Cycle 1: run-up 1930-45, wartime default, low debt to 1970
Big Debt Cycle 2: leveraging 1970-89, bubble, 1989-90 bust
1990-2013: non-deleveraging, deflation ('exactly what not to do')
now: stimulative pushing on a string with large BoJ balance-sheet risk; debt service/revenue rising toward but below the 150% bust threshold
lessons: Beautiful deleveraging requires prompt restructuring plus rates held below nominal growth and inflation plus monetization; Japan delayed restructuring nine years and the rate condition 23 years (p. 289, 293)
Three arrows (money, fiscal, reform) are classically the best policies against deflationary depression (p. 294)
Do not own government bonds amid extreme monetization (p. 295)
Monetization plus depreciation taxes bondholders and savers; yen holdings lost more than half their value, 'not dissimilar to a default' (p. 309)
Debt can be deleveraged in foreign-currency and gold terms while rising in local currency (debt in gold -82% since 2001) (p. 310)
Hedged domestic JGB holders did OK; weak economy kept yen weakness from becoming domestic inflation (p. 311)
Depreciation makes the country competitive (wages, home prices, FDI, P/E) (p. 312-313)
BoJ losses would be huge if rates normalize: 3% real-rate rise -> ~30% GDP MTM loss, -2.5% GDP cash flow, deficit 4% -> 8%, debt 220% -> 300% over 20 years, 5-6% GDP/yr combined need (p. 299)
Debt busts historically occurred when debt service exceeded 150% of revenue (p. 314)
Non-tradables stayed affordable in labor terms while tradables soared; the composition of inflation, not its average, reveals the winners and losers (p. 301)
analogies_to_today: Offered as the case study for the US, China and Europe (p. 293); Chinese policy makers urged to read it (p. 288)
Pre-WWII sanctions on Japan compared to the US-China conflict today (p. 291)
Japan is now preparing for war with China as the US's main regional ally (p. 306)
BoJ monetary base ~5x the Fed's, so central-bank losses could be much larger than the Fed's ~0.5% of GDP (p. 317)

parts: Spending cuts (about 4% of spending in the balanced version; about 6% if the Fed does not cooperate)
Tax increases (about 4% of tax revenue in the balanced version; about 6% if the Fed does not cooperate)
Interest-rate cuts (about 1% cut in real interest rates; the most impactful lever)

Cut when economic conditions are good so the cuts are counter-cyclical; do it now while the US is near full employment with strong private balance sheets (pp. 342, 353)
Have monetary policy stimulative enough to keep the economy strong; fiscal tightening paired with monetary easing (pp. 339, 342)
Debts must be in a currency the central bank can print (p. 342)
Phase in over three years to avoid abrupt changes (p. 340)
Adopt as a bipartisan fallback that triggers automatically if no better plan is agreed; a bipartisan fiscal commission may then propose alternatives (pp. 336, 348)
Protect those least able to afford cuts and high-productivity functions such as education; cut taxes/regulations that free productive activity (fn 52, p. 348)
If the 2017 tax cuts are extended, the required cut rises to over 4% of GDP (p. 342)
Combine with a coordinated 'beautiful deleveraging' balancing deflationary and inflationary deleveraging tools (p. 367)
Also consider marking government assets to market, a US sovereign wealth fund and a US-backed stablecoin (p. 354)
