principles.text: Agreeing on how things work is a precondition for agreeing on what is happening or likely to happen.
The credit/spending/debt-paying-back dynamic is inherently cyclical.

A debt is a promise to deliver money; a debt crisis is more promises than money; the central bank must print (devalue) or not print (default crisis) and in the end always prints and devalues; either way too much debt makes debt assets worth less.
There is always a popular meme nearly everyone believes that is in the price and bound to be wrong in some way; investors extrapolate, act emotionally, ignore pricing, bet on rises and use leverage.
Net selling of debt assets, especially government debt assets, is a big red flag.

When rates rise the central bank loses money on its bonds because it pays more on its liabilities than it earns; this becomes a big red flag only when net worth is very negative and it must print to cover negative cash flow.
Big debt crises are inevitable.
Build up savings in good times to draw on in bad times; too much and too little saving both have costs and nobody gets the balance exactly right.
Anticipate debt crises by understanding a number of interrelated dynamics, not a single number like debt as a percent of GDP.
If debts are in the country's own currency, the central bank can and will print money to alleviate the crisis, which reduces the value of the money.
All debt crises, even big ones, can be managed well by balancing deflationary restructuring with inflationary monetization; the key is spreading the paying back over time.
Debt crises provide great risks and great opportunities: they have destroyed empires and rewarded investors who understand them.

The five most important drivers of change are the debt/credit/money/economic cycle, the internal political order/disorder cycle, the external geopolitical order/disorder cycle, acts of nature and human inventiveness (new technologies).
All markets and economies are simply the aggregates of the transactions that make them up.
Price equals the money/credit the buyer gives divided by the quantity the seller gives; a market is the aggregate of those transactions.
Price (P) = amount spent ($) / total quantity sold (Q); P = $/Q.
Knowing total spending and total quantity sold tells you the price and everything else you need to know.
Identifying unsustainable rates of buying and/or selling identifies unsustainable prices and economic conditions.
When more money and credit are created and producers have capacity, there is non-inflationary growth because both spending and quantity rise.
When more money and credit are created but producers lack capacity, there is little real growth and much more inflation.
People buy goods and services to use and investments to make money (as storeholds of wealth).
What people spend on is based on the relative appeal of items, compared one against another and over time.
Currencies are mediums of exchange and storeholds of wealth (in debt assets).
Investments are exchanges of money and credit today for money and credit in the future.
All investment markets derive value from yields and price changes; total return = yield + price change.
All investment markets compete on total return because investors care about total return more than its form and can arbitrage between investments.
Expected real returns relative to inflation determine how much money flows into each investment.
Prices are linked by determinants (spot/forward relationships) that one must understand to understand relative pricing.
Debt and currency are essentially the same thing; if you don't like one you must not like the other.
Five types of players drive money and debt cycles: borrower-debtors, lender-creditors, banks, central governments and central banks.
Debt/credit expansion can only happen when both borrowers and lenders are willing, so the deal must be good for both.
Over the long run debts cannot rise faster than the incomes that service them, and rates cannot be too high for borrowers or too low for lenders for very long.
Big debt crises come when debt assets and liabilities become too large relative to money and/or goods and services in existence.
Central banks want to keep debt growth, economic growth and inflation at acceptable levels.
Central governments are political organizations whose leaders serve elected officials, so they want to give people what they want.
The greater debt assets and liabilities are relative to real incomes, the harder the balancing act between lenders and borrowers and the likelier a debt-caused downturn.
The short-term debt cycles add up to the long-term (big) debt cycle, the Big Debt Cycle.
A debt cycle is sustainable only if the debt creates sufficient income to pay the debt service; otherwise debt-to-income grows mechanically and borrowing is needed to service debt.
A sure sign of moving toward a debt crisis is a large and rising amount of borrowing used to pay debt service.

Debt isn't always bad even when uneconomic; too little credit can be as harmful as too much, and losses can be spread tolerably if the government controls restructuring and the debt is in a printable currency.
From one cycle to the next debt liabilities and assets have virtually always increased until burdens became unsustainably large or debt assets intolerably low-returning.
Goods, services and investment assets can be produced, bought and sold with money and credit.
Central banks can produce money and influence the amount of credit in whatever quantities they want.
Borrower-debtors require enough money and low enough rates to borrow and service their debts.
Lender-creditors require high enough rates and low enough default rates to earn adequate returns.
The balancing act gets progressively harder as debt assets and liabilities rise relative to incomes; eventually they must be reduced, so a deleveraging happens.
The best deleveraging is a beautiful one, which governments and central banks can engineer when debts are in their own currency; foreign-currency debt makes deleveraging ugly.
Over the long term, productivity, healthy income statements (earning more than spending) and healthy balance sheets (more assets than liabilities) mark financial health.
If you know where each country is in the debt/credit cycle and how players are likely to behave, you can navigate the cycles well.
The past is prologue.
Debt crises are inevitable; only a few well-disciplined countries have avoided them because lending is never done perfectly and psychology produces bubbles and busts.
Most debt crises, even big ones, can be managed well if policy makers spread out their negative impacts.
All debt crises provide investment opportunities to investors who understand them and have good principles for navigating them.

At the beginning of the end of the Big Debt Cycle real rates cannot satisfy both lenders and borrowers; both tight-money contraction and loose-money inflation occur, only the order is uncertain, and owning the debt/currency of overly indebted governments is then a bad investment.

Central banks must choose between hard money (defaults, deflationary depressions) and soft money (printing, devaluing money and debt); they always eventually print and devalue, and each can print only its own currency.
If debts are in a country's own currency its central bank can and will print to alleviate the crisis, managing it better but reducing the value of the money.

An unsustainable debt burden exists when inflows are less than outflows so that savings fall and/or borrowing rises until savings run out and/or borrowing is impossible, at which point a debt failure occurs.

Equilibrium levels of debt/income, debt service/income, nominal rates versus inflation and growth, and debt/savings will be approached; the ratios go to extremes and return one way or another, and the deleveraging can be handled well or badly.
Countries with very high debt levels, very large deficits, low savings and very high, fast-rising interest rates have a very high risk of a debt default or devaluation crisis.
If nominal rates equal nominal income growth and there is no primary deficit, debt stays constant relative to income; if rates exceed income growth, existing debt burdens increase.
Accumulating debt service is like plaque in the arteries, squeezing out the flow of nutrients to the economy.
The main effect of high debt levels is making the debtor vulnerable to being unable to roll the debt forward.
The easiest, though not best, path is for governments to have the central bank print and buy bonds to hold rates down and fund spending; they unfailingly do this when debts are in their own currency.
Buying up bonds and increasing the money supply are stimulative and put downward pressure on the currency.

Decision rules should rest on timeless, universal cause/effect relationships that explain all big developments in every time frame and country; if a rule fails to explain some big development, an influence is missing and must be added to the template.

A newly chosen leader enjoys a honeymoon of optimism (e.g., the first 100 days); then promises prove hard to keep, disappointment sets in, critics grow bolder, support wanes, and holding power gets harder, which often drives more extreme actions.
When democracies fail, autocracies come in.
In times of disorder, financial, political and military power count for more than laws, and authoritarianism outperforms weak, disorganized collectivism.
Power corrupts, and absolute power corrupts absolutely (attributed to Lord Acton, 1887).
The strong prey on the weak - the operating rule once the pendulum swings to unilateralism.
Alliances change fast when circumstances change fast, because winning matters more than loyalty.
Civility taken too far breeds weak decadence that eventually loses to strong barbarism.
The biggest and most important force is how people deal with each other.

To see how and why big events unfolded, do not focus on small events; those who look up close and precisely miss the most important big things, so when looking for big things pay attention to big things

Everything happens for reasons; strive to understand the cause/effect relationships and build a logical template that explains past changes and matches what is actually happening, resolving any discrepancies

When debt is too large relative to the money needed to service it, governments break their promises through some mix of (a) creating more money and credit, (b) reducing debt (e.g., restructuring), and (c) restricting free ownership and movement of hard money; a run from bad money to good money follows, which governments try to stop by banning good money
When countries are weak, opposing countries take advantage of their weaknesses to obtain gains

Central banks stimulate by cutting rates and/or creating money and credit, extending the expansion while raising debt relative to income; when they can no longer cut rates they print money and buy debt, especially government debt, so debtors can keep borrowing until debt assets and liabilities become too great to balance, at which point restructuring and/or monetization must occur

The relationship between interest rates and inflation matters: rates high relative to inflation reward saving and lending, rates low relative to inflation reward borrowing and holding assets that benefit from inflation and growth
The yield curve matters: short rates high relative to long rates mean tight money and make holding and lending cash more attractive than borrowing and investing in other assets
When a debt problem is intolerably painful, central banks will print money and distribute it to make debts easier to pay, which devalues money and debt relative to other assets
Everything seems bigger up close

Great companies in great industries are not automatically great investments because price matters; bubbles form when such thinking is leveraged with borrowing and typically burst when central banks tighten and rates rise
Do not own government bonds when there are extreme amounts of debt monetization

When large, fast-growing government debts require big deficit cuts: cut by enough to fix the problem; cut when economic conditions are good so the cuts are counter-cyclical; keep monetary policy stimulative enough to hold the economy up.

When there is too much debt relative to the money needed to service it, governments break promises through some mix of creating more money and credit, reducing debt by restructuring, and blocking free ownership and movement of hard money such as gold; a run from bad money to good money follows and governments try to stop it by prohibiting good money from being freely held or moved.

There is always a dominant popular meme that is already in the price and bound to be wrong in some way; it comes from extrapolation and emotion; most investors judge an investment great without weighing its price, and most are long, often with leverage.
Globalization is an unstoppable force.

A newly elected leader enjoys a honeymoon of optimism (e.g., the first 100 days); as promises prove hard to deliver, disappointment sets in, critics grow bolder, support wanes, and staying in power requires more extreme actions.
When democracies fail, autocracies come in.
In times of disorder, financial, political and military power matter more than laws, and authoritarianism works better than weak, disorganized collectivism.
New leaders in periods of great conflict take steps to consolidate power; the more autocratic do so more forcefully.

In great conflicts, aggressive leaders eliminate the opposition through threats and damaging actions, legal changes granting themselves special powers, and control of the media for propaganda; if conflict becomes severe, laws and punishments targeting the opposition follow.
To be successful, a system must produce adequate conditions for most people.
The strong prey on the weak.
Alliances change fast when circumstances change quickly, because winning matters more than loyalty.
By and large, intellectual property protections don't work; assume openly shown good ideas are replicated in about six months.
The biggest, most important force is how people deal with each other.
If you're not worried, you need to worry; if you're worried, you don't need to worry — worrying about what can go wrong protects you.

non_red_dot_rules.text: The nine-item checklist is a risk gauge: the more of the unhealthy conditions present, the higher the probability of a debt/currency crisis ('heart attack').
Big net selling of government debt is the big red flag; stage 4 shows as rates rising, long rates leading, with the currency weakening at the same time.
Private debt falling sharply while government debt rises sharply is a short leading indicator of trouble.
Government debt service near 100% of income is a red flag.
Debts rising relative to incomes until smart investors see losses as inevitable is a relatively large red flag.
The central bank will always choose printing over letting rates clear the market; the best path balances the two.
Watch reserve and sovereign-wealth-fund size, drawdown speed and distance from empty for timing; selling FX to buy local currency is a tightening.
Foreign outflows classically lead the devaluation.
Long-running QE, maturity shortening and a rising central-bank share of government debt are early-stage red flags that begin about a decade before the crisis.
Central-bank losses are a flag; negative net worth a moderate flag; printing to cover negative cash flow the big red flag.
Gold beats local cash by roughly 60% on average from devaluation start to currency bottom.
Once the stage-9 conditions (restructured debt, fiscal adjustment, reserves, high real rates, central-bank limits) are met, it is among the best times to hold the currency and debt.
Fiat devaluations are gradual, hard-money devaluations abrupt; reserve-currency issuers tend to over-borrow and fall more abruptly.
